query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, trace amount of an interstitial element such as boron into a MoNbTaW‐based refractory high‐entropy alloy will strengthen its grain boundaries and pin dislocations, thereby enhancing its high‐temperature yield strength without significantly increasing density or degrading room‐temperature ductility. This effect is achieved by promoting local lattice distortions and improved grain-boundary cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: An undoped MoNbTaW refractory high‐entropy alloy currently exhibiting excellent room-temperature yield strength and reasonable ductility but limited high-temperature compressive capability.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a trace level of boron into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted under high operating temperatures typical of jet-turbine applications as well as at room temperature to assess ductility and strength.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion through boron segregation and the formation of fine boride precipitates that impede dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: The trace boron doping induces local lattice distortions and reinforces grain boundary cohesion, thereby pinning dislocations and delaying dislocation mobility at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the undoped MoNbTaW alloy, the boron-doped variant will demonstrate a measurable increase in high-temperature yield strength (potentially on the order of 10–20% improvement), while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility and only a negligible increase in density.
generation.baseline: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy without boron doping.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a narrow dopant range; excessive boron may cause unwanted brittleness or formation of large precipitates, so the optimized interstitial content is crucial.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the high-temperature strength improvement and its correlation with the optimal boron concentration remain to be precisely determined through systematic experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy: one set as a control (undoped) and the other with trace (0.1–0.5 at%) boron doping. Subject both sets to identical fabrication processes (melting, mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering, etc.). Conduct compressive and tensile mechanical tests at room temperature and at high temperatures (e.g., 1200–1600 °C) to measure yield strength, ductility, and density. Use microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, SEM, or APT) to verify the boron distribution and any boride formation.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength (compressive and/or tensile tests)
Microstructural characterization (grain boundary features, precipitate size/distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >10%) improvement in high-temperature yield strength compared to the undoped control, or if it shows a marked decrease in room-temperature ductility or an unacceptable density increase, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.
